Smart India Hackathon 2026 · Problem Statement SIH26164

CryptoDrishti

An enterprise cryptographic discovery and quantum-risk analysis tool. It finds every piece of cryptography an organisation actually runs, scores how long that data survives a quantum computer, and emits the result as a standards-conformant cryptographic bill of materials.

SIH26164 NTRO Blockchain & Cybersecurity Software Fully offline / air-gap capable
How to use this document. Sections 01–16 are the complete record of the project. Section 17 is the build kit — it maps this content onto the six slides of the official SIH template, with copy you can paste directly and a note on which screenshot belongs where. Start there if you are building the deck.

01

Executive summary

Every organisation runs cryptography it cannot enumerate — in source code, in compiled binaries, in certificates, in config files, on live ports. Quantum computers break most of it. Before anyone can migrate, they need an inventory, and no such inventory exists today.

CryptoDrishti produces that inventory automatically. Point it at a codebase, a tree of binaries, a certificate store or a live endpoint; six independent sensors read what is actually there; the engine classifies every asset by what a quantum computer does to it, scores it, and reports how many years of exposure the organisation is carrying. The output is a CycloneDX 1.6 CBOM — the ECMA-424 standard — that a regulator or downstream tool can consume directly.

Those are real measured numbers from scanning the OpenSSL codebase — the library that secures most of the internet — not a prepared sample. 2,102 raw detector hits grouped into 77 distinct cryptographic assets across six sensors.

02

The problem statement

SIH26164, issued by the National Technical Research Organisation (NTRO), asks for an enterprise tool that does four things. Each clause is a hard requirement, and each maps to a part of what we built.

#The clause asks forHow CryptoDrishti answers it
iDiscover cryptographic assets across an enterprise — source, binaries, certificates, protocolsSix independent sensors, each reading a different surface. No single technique is trusted alone.
iiAnalyse and classify them by quantum vulnerability52-algorithm knowledge base mapping each to Shor-broken, Grover-weakened, hybrid, quantum-safe or unresolved.
iiiQuantify risk and prioritise remediationQuantum Risk Score plus Mosca's inequality over a Q-Day distribution, producing years-of-exposure per asset.
ivRecommend post-quantum alternatives by risk profile, latency and costConstrained recommender using real key and signature sizes across four deployment profiles.
vOutput a standardised CBOM and an interactive GUICycloneDX 1.6 / ECMA-424 emitter with live structural validation, and a browser console with no build step.

03

Why this matters

The two algorithms that break everything

Shor's algorithm factors large integers and solves discrete logarithms in polynomial time. That destroys RSA, Diffie–Hellman, ECDH and ECDSA outright — not weakens them, ends them. Grover's algorithm halves the effective strength of symmetric ciphers and hashes, so AES-128 drops to about 64 bits of security and needs to become AES-256.

Harvest now, decrypt later

An adversary does not need a quantum computer today to benefit from one tomorrow. They record encrypted traffic now and decrypt it when the machine arrives. Any data whose secrecy must outlive Q-Day is already compromised. This is why an inventory cannot wait for the hardware.

Mosca's inequality

Michele Mosca's formulation is the standard way this risk is stated. If X + Y > Z — where X is how long the data must stay secret, Y is how long migration takes, and Z is the years until a quantum computer exists — then data recorded today is readable before you have finished migrating. Our tool computes this per asset.

The Indian mandate

This is not speculative policy. The DST / National Quantum Mission report Implementation of a Quantum Safe Ecosystem in India (February 2026, with CERT-In) sets a dated national timeline:

ByRequirement
Dec 2026PQC certification labs established
Dec 2027Cryptographic inventories across defence, power, telecom and BFSI
Dec 2028Priority migration begins
Dec 2029Full PQC transition

The December 2027 line is the one that matters. A cryptographic inventory across four national sectors is a mandate with a date on it, and there is no tool to produce one. That is precisely the gap this fills.

Internationally the deadlines are equally firm. NIST IR 8547 deprecates RSA-2048 and ECC P-256 in 2030 and disallows them in 2035. FIPS 203, 204 and 205 standardised ML-KEM, ML-DSA and SLH-DSA in August 2024; HQC was selected in March 2025.

04

What we built

A single-binary local web application. You open it, aim it at a path, and it reports. There is no cloud service, no account, no build step and no external request of any kind — you can unplug the network cable and it works identically.

Design principle: colour means exactly one thing

The interface chrome is entirely achromatic — bone and graphite, with primary actions rendered as inverted ink rather than a tinted accent. The only colour anywhere on the page is the five quantum-exposure classes. That is a deliberate constraint: when a reviewer sees colour, it is always carrying meaning, never decoration.

ClassMeaningExample algorithmsAction
Broken by ShorDestroyed outright by a quantum computerRSA, DH, ECDH, ECDSA, DSAReplace with ML-KEM / ML-DSA
Weakened by GroverEffective strength halvedAES-128, SHA-256, 3DESDouble the key / widen the hash
UnresolvedCould not be determined staticallyOpaque key material, indirect callsManual review — never guessed
HybridClassical + PQC; safe if either holdsX25519+ML-KEM-768Current recommended posture
Quantum-safeBelieved secure post-quantumML-KEM, ML-DSA, SLH-DSA, AES-256Record as compliant

Both colour sets were validated for colour-blind separation with a perceptual checker rather than chosen by eye — light mode scores 11.4 (deuteranopia), 11.4 (tritanopia) and 19.3 (normal vision) on adjacent-pair separation; dark mode scores 14.8, 18.2 and 21.0, all passing contrast against their own surface. Class is never encoded by colour alone; every mark, row and key entry is also labelled.

05

Architecture

The pipeline is deliberately linear and inspectable. Each stage has one job and hands a typed structure to the next.

STAGE 1

Sensors

Six independent readers produce raw findings with evidence — file, line, matched symbol, technique, confidence.

STAGE 2

Normalise

2,102 raw hits collapse into 77 distinct assets. Evidence is merged and confidence fused; an inventory that lists one algorithm 300 times is a log, not an inventory.

STAGE 3

Classify & score

Each asset resolved against the 52-algorithm knowledge base, then scored: quantum class, key size, context, reachability, Mosca exposure.

STAGE 4

Recommend

A migration target chosen per asset under the selected deployment profile, with the real byte cost stated.

STAGE 5

Emit

CycloneDX 1.6 CBOM, printable assessment report, and the interactive console.

Module map

PathResponsibility
app/scanners/source, deps, certs, configs, binary, network — the six sensors
app/knowledge/algorithm registry, source rule pack, binary constants and symbols
app/engine/normalize, risk (scoring + Mosca), recommend
app/cbom.pyCycloneDX 1.6 emitter and structural validator
app/api.py13 HTTP routes; scans run on a background thread with live progress
app/web/the console — plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript, no framework
run.pysingle entry point: --seed, --preflight, --demo-reset

07

Detection: the six sensors

Cryptography hides in different places and no single technique finds all of it. Each sensor reads a different surface and reports its own evidence.

#SensorTechniqueCoverage
01SourcePython ast parsing for .py; a curated rule pack for the rest49 rules, 9 languages
02DependencyManifests resolved to what crypto each library can actually performpip, npm, Maven, Go, Cargo
03CertificateX.509 parsed for key type, size, validity and signature algorithmincl. ML-DSA / ML-KEM / SLH-DSA OIDs
04ConfigurationTLS, SSH and IPsec parameters as actually deployedcipher suites, groups, versions
05BinaryELF symbol tables plus byte-matching of verified crypto constants8 constants, 72 symbols, 9 version patterns
06NetworkLive TLS handshake against a real endpoint, including hybrid PQC group supportthree-state: supported / not / untested

Why the binary sensor is the differentiator

Source scanning only finds code you have. Most enterprises run vendor binaries they cannot read. The binary sensor searches compiled files for the actual constant tables that cryptographic implementations must contain — the AES S-box, the SHA-256 round constants, the MD5 T-table. Those bytes cannot be obfuscated away without breaking the algorithm.

Two real bugs we caught, and how. We recomputed every constant table from first principles and matched them against a real libcrypto binary. That found two hex typos in our own tables — the MD5 T-table and a SHA-1 round constant — which would have silently produced false negatives. We also removed a 4-byte DES signature that matched 32 unrelated system binaries, and an unverified Kyber constant table. An unverified signature is worse than a missing one, because it produces confident wrong answers.

Honesty about precision

Regex-based detection for non-Python languages has lower precision than AST analysis. We say so in the interface rather than hiding it: every finding carries a confidence score, and anything that cannot be resolved statically is reported as Unresolved rather than guessed. In front of cryptographers, a confident wrong answer is worse than an honest gap.

08

The risk engine

Quantum Risk Score

Every asset receives a score from 0 to 100 composed of named factors, all of which are shown in the interface so a reviewer can audit the arithmetic: quantum class, classical key strength, deployment context (production / test / vendored), how many places use it, detection confidence, standards deprecation dates from NIST IR 8547, and the Mosca exposure term. Bands are medium at 25, high at 45, critical at 70.

Mosca over a distribution, not a date

Nobody knows when a cryptanalytically relevant quantum computer arrives, so the tool does not assert a date. Q-Day is modelled as a distribution over 2030 / 2034 / 2044 (earliest / likely / latest), the defaults following the Global Risk Institute's expert-survey range, and every one is adjustable live.

SensitivityX — secrecy lifetimeTypical use
Restricted25 yrDefence, national security classification
Confidential10 yrCommercial, financial records
Internal5 yrBusiness operations
Public1 yrNothing sensitive

The demonstration moment. Moving Q-Day from 2034 to 2030 and switching sensitivity to restricted takes peak exposure from 4.5 years to 23.5 years and moves 23 assets from medium to high. That recalculation is what a CISO takes to a budget committee, and it happens live in about 100 ms.

09

Recommendation engine

Clause (iv) asks for alternatives selected by risk profile, latency and cost. That is a constrained choice, not a lookup — and the constraint that dominates is size.

An ECDSA P-256 signature is 64 bytes. ML-DSA-65 is 3,309. On a TLS handshake that is invisible; on a constrained radio link with a 51-byte payload it is impossible, and recommending it there would be wrong. The engine reasons about the size delta and says so — including when the honest answer is that no drop-in replacement exists and the device needs a hardware refresh.

ProfileKey establishmentSignaturesReasoning
General purposeX25519 + ML-KEM-768 (hybrid)ML-DSA-65Current mainstream posture; already negotiated by browsers and OpenSSL 3.5+
High assuranceML-KEM-1024ML-DSA-87Category 5 parameters for material that must outlive Q-Day comfortably
Constrained / IoTML-KEM-512FN-DSA-512Smallest standardised sets; flagged where the link budget still cannot carry it
Firmware signing—SLH-DSA-128sHash-based, resting only on the hash function — the most conservative assumption available

The engine also recommends crypto-agility, not only an algorithm: a hardcoded call site will need replacing again at the next transition, so it advises routing key establishment through a provider interface.

Scan performance

Scan time scales with per-file work, not just file count. A full Python AST parse costs roughly five times a regex pass, so Python-heavy targets are slower:

TargetFilesTimeRate
OpenSSL (mostly C)2,1627.8 s~280 files/s
Django (mostly Python)3,043~56 s~54 files/s

Preflight. python run.py --preflight runs 15 self-checks — database, seeded scan, CBOM validity, Q-Day round trip, demo repositories, binary target, air-gap grep, presenter kit, live probe availability — and reports ALL CLEAR before you walk on stage.

14

Feasibility, risks and honest limits

Stating limitations before a judge finds them is a strength. Each of these has a mitigation already implemented.

LimitationWhy it existsMitigation in the build
Regex precision below ASTOnly Python has a native parser in the standard libraryConfidence score on every finding; unresolvable cases marked Unresolved, never guessed
Binary detection is signature-basedCannot symbolically execute a stripped binaryOnly constants verified against real libcrypto are shipped; unverified ones were deliberately removed
Q-Day is unknowableIt is a genuine open questionModelled as a distribution and reported as a probability; never asserted as a date
Scan time on very large estatesPer-file AST parsing is CPU boundFile-count cap, parallel workers, live progress, and a pre-seeded scan so a demo never waits
Dynamic / reflective crypto callsStatic analysis cannot resolve runtime dispatchReported as Unresolved with the call site, for manual review
No agent on remote hosts yetScope for the hackathon buildThe network sensor already probes live endpoints; a collector agent is the natural next step

Why it is deployable, not just a demo

  • Four dependencies. The entire supply chain fits on one line — which matters enormously for accreditation in a classified environment.
  • No network egress. It can be installed inside an air-gapped enclave with no exception request.
  • Single file database. Nothing to provision; results are portable.
  • Standards output. The CBOM plugs into existing SBOM tooling rather than requiring anyone to adopt our format.

15

Impact and benefits

For NTRO and national security

  • Produces the cryptographic inventory the National Quantum Mission requires across defence, power, telecom and BFSI by December 2027.
  • Quantifies harvest-now-decrypt-later exposure in years, so classified material with a 25-year secrecy requirement can be prioritised first.
  • Runs air-gapped, which is the only way a tool like this is usable inside a classified enclave.

Economic

  • Migration is grouped into workstreams by replacement algorithm, which is how the work is actually staffed and costed — turning an unbounded programme into a finite one.
  • Surfacing byte-size deltas before rollout prevents the expensive class of failure where a signature no longer fits a fixed-width protocol field discovered in production.
  • Avoids the far greater cost of an unplanned emergency migration after a cryptographic break.

Strategic and social

  • Supports Indian cryptographic sovereignty: an indigenous tool for an indigenous mandate, with no foreign cloud dependency.
  • The interface teaches while it reports — the sensor array and the Notes layer explain the reasoning, so it builds institutional PQC literacy rather than requiring it.
  • Standards-conformant output means findings are portable between agencies and vendors.

SLIDE 2

Proposed solution — idea, innovation, uniqueness

Detailed explanation of the proposed solution — paste this

CryptoDrishti is an offline enterprise tool that discovers every cryptographic asset an organisation actually runs and reports how long that data survives a quantum computer. Six independent sensors read source code, dependency manifests, X.509 certificates, deployed configuration, compiled binaries and live TLS endpoints. Raw detections are grouped into distinct assets, classified against a 52-algorithm knowledge base, and scored with Mosca's inequality over a Q-Day probability distribution. The output is a CycloneDX 1.6 (ECMA-424) cryptographic bill of materials, validated live, plus a per-asset migration target with its real byte cost.

How it addresses the problem

  • The National Quantum Mission requires cryptographic inventories across defence, power, telecom and BFSI by December 2027. No tool exists to produce one.
  • Migration cannot begin without an inventory; this produces it automatically in seconds.
  • It answers all five clauses of the problem statement, not only discovery.

Innovation and uniqueness — the four lines that differentiate

  • Binary sensor. Finds crypto in vendor binaries you cannot read, by matching verified constant tables (AES S-box, SHA-256 round constants) that cannot be obfuscated without breaking the algorithm.
  • Exposure in years, not a severity label. Mosca over a Q-Day distribution gives “4.5 years readable” instead of “high”.
  • Recommendations constrained by size. ECDSA is 64 bytes, ML-DSA-65 is 3,309 — the engine refuses to recommend what a constrained link cannot carry.
  • Zero external requests. Demonstrated by unplugging the network cable mid-demo.

Visual to use

The console screenshot (section 11, first image) — it shows the product and the six sensors in one frame.
